findings.reason: The title 'widow's tax trap' is gendered jargon. Retitled 'Plan for the survivor's tax squeeze' as suggested. This is a title-only change, outside the body/plain gate.

Two of the three clocks are already in the pause body ('the COBRA and Marketplace windows begin when that coverage ends' and 'a decision to disclaim an inheritance must generally be made within 9 months and before you accept the asset'). Portability was missing and is added. The return must be filed for portability whatever the estate's size (§2010(c)(5)(A); Form 706 instructions), and it is due 9 months after the death (§6075(a)), subject to extension. Not added, to keep the step short: the reviewer's 'up to 5 years' late-election relief and 'COBRA up to 36 months'. The checker read both today and both are correct: the Form 706 instructions give the fifth anniversary for executors with no other filing requirement, and 29 U.S.C. §1162(2)(A)(iv) with §1163(1) gives 36 months after the covered employee's death. Either can be added if the owner wants. The sentence tells the reader to ask a professional rather than setting a size threshold.

It uses the existing {{fig:sec121_exclusion_mfj}} token. IRMAA: the single-filer threshold is half the joint one (§1395r(i)(2)). findings.reason: The point stands: acceptance bars a qualified disclaimer. But the reviewer's 'claiming or re-titling counts as accepting' overstates it. Treas. Reg. §25.2518-2(d)(1) says merely taking delivery of title does not count. The new sentence uses the regulation's own list of acts that indicate acceptance, and says they 'can count'.

sources.quote: Acts indicative of acceptance include using the property or the interest in property; accepting dividends, interest, or rents from the property; and directing others to act with respect to the property or interest in property.
However, merely taking delivery of an instrument of title, without more, does not constitute acceptance.

blocks.body: A few clocks start now, and the rest can wait. If your health coverage came through your spouse's employer, the COBRA and Marketplace windows begin when that coverage ends (60 days to act), and a decision to disclaim an inheritance must generally be made within 9 months and before you accept the asset. Ask a tax preparer or estate attorney whether to file an estate-tax return for your spouse (generally due in 9 months); it can pass their unused exemption to you even when no tax is owed. If a collector asks you to pay your spouse's debts, don't use your own money until you check: the estate generally pays them, and you usually owe only debts you co-signed or held jointly (being an authorized user is not joint) or ones your state's law puts on a surviving spouse. Selling the house, moving, or taking a lump sum can wait. Locate the will, policies and account statements, and get several certified copies of the death certificate — most institutions ask for one.
blocks.plain: A few clocks start now, and the rest can wait. If your health insurance came through your spouse's job, the COBRA and Marketplace windows start when that coverage ends (you have 60 days to act), and if you want to turn down an inheritance you generally must do it within 9 months and before you accept it. Ask a tax preparer or estate lawyer whether to file an estate tax return for your spouse (usually due in 9 months). It can pass your spouse's unused exemption to you even when no tax is owed. If a debt collector asks you to pay your spouse's debts, don't use your own money until you check. The estate usually pays them. You usually owe only debts that were joint or that you co-signed (being an authorized user on a card is not joint), or debts your state's law makes a surviving spouse pay. Selling the house, moving, or taking a lump sum can wait. Find the will, insurance policies and account statements, and get several certified copies of the death certificate — most companies will ask for one.

Irreversible moves (sell house, move, lump sum) can wait
Get several certified death certificates; most institutions ask for one
COBRA and Marketplace windows start at loss of spouse-employer coverage; 60 days
A disclaimer must generally be made within 9 months and before accepting the asset
Ask whether to file an estate-tax return for the spouse (generally due in 9 months); it can pass the unused exemption even when no tax is owed
If a collector asks you to pay the spouse's debts, do not use your own money until you have checked
The estate generally pays the debts; you usually owe only joint or co-signed debts (an authorized user is not joint) or ones state law puts on a surviving spouse

blocks.body: Report the death to the Social Security Administration (funeral homes often do this). A surviving spouse can receive survivor benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled), and at any age while not remarried and caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and entitled to child's benefits; the children themselves can receive benefits while under 18 (19 if still in secondary school), and there is a one-time lump-sum death payment. Switching between your own and the survivor benefit later can be worth comparing.
blocks.plain: Tell the Social Security Administration about the death (the funeral home often does this). A surviving spouse can get survivor benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled), and at any age if they have not remarried and are caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and qualifies for child's benefits. The children can get benefits of their own while under 18 (19 if still in high school), and there is a one-time lump-sum death payment. Later, you may be able to switch between the survivor benefit and your own; compare which pays more and when.
props: Report the death to SSA; funeral homes often do
Switching between own and survivor benefit later is worth comparing
Age 50 if disabled; any age while caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and entitled to child's benefits
Children receive benefits under 18 (19 if a secondary-school student)
There is a one-time lump-sum death payment
The any-age benefit requires that the surviving spouse has not remarried
blocks.notes: Lean text equals the full proposal: the one-clause addition 'under 16 or disabled' is the ADV-46 (HIGH) fix. It also covers CFP-46 (MED), which asks for the same clause, and it corrects a factual error in the current text: 'child who is entitled to child's benefits' would cover a 16- or 17-year-old, who under 42 U.S.C. 402(s)(1) does not qualify the parent for the any-age benefit. Reconciled 2026-11-16 with the factual corrections on branch fix/verification-2026-11-16.

blocks.body: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay to the named beneficiary directly. A surviving spouse who inherits an IRA can treat it as their own, roll it over, or keep it as an inherited IRA — the choice matters if the survivor is under 59½.
blocks.plain: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay the named beneficiary directly. A surviving spouse who inherits an IRA can treat it as their own, roll it over, or keep it as an inherited IRA. The choice matters if the surviving spouse is under 59½.

blocks.body: You can still file jointly for the year of death. After that, a survivor with a dependent child can file as a qualifying surviving spouse for two more years; otherwise the survivor files single — often with similar income but narrower brackets. Inherited assets generally receive a stepped-up basis, and in community-property states both halves of community property can.
blocks.plain: You can still file a joint return for the year your spouse died. After that, if you have a dependent child, you can file as a qualifying surviving spouse for two more years. Otherwise you file as single — often with about the same income but narrower tax brackets. Inherited assets usually get a stepped-up cost basis, and in community-property states both halves of shared property can.

new_claims.claim: A deceased spouse's unused estate-tax exclusion (DSUE) can be used by the surviving spouse only if the executor elects portability on a timely filed estate-tax return (due 9 months after death, plus extensions); a return is required to elect regardless of the size of the estate
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: §2010(c)(5)(A) (DSUE amount may not be taken into account 'unless the executor of the estate of the deceased spouse files an estate tax return on which such amount is computed and makes an election'; no election if filed after the time prescribed, including extensions); §6075(a) ('shall be filed within 9 months after the date of the decedent's death'); Form 706 instructions ('The filing requirement applies to all estates of decedents choosing to elect portability of the DSUE amount, regardless of the size of the estate'). Late-election relief read in the Form 706 instructions 2026-11-16 ('Executors filing to elect portability may now file Form 706 on or before the fifth anniversary of the decedent's death', for executors with no filing requirement under §6018(a), per Rev. Proc. 2022-32); not used in block text. Added 2026-11-16 from the §4.4 persona pass (CFP-45).

new_claims.claim: A deceased person's debts are generally paid from the estate; a surviving spouse is not personally responsible unless a co-signer, a joint account holder (not an authorized user), or obligated by state law, including community-property states that require jointly held property to be used
new_claims.source: CFPB 'A debt collector is trying to collect a debt of a deceased relative. What can I do?' (last reviewed Oct 15, 2026)
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: CFPB lists the exceptions (co-signer; joint account holder on a credit card, 'different from an authorized user'; surviving spouse where state law requires paying a particular type of debt; executor rules; community-property states requiring jointly held property to pay a deceased spouse's debts) and says collectors may not imply a survivor must pay from their own assets. State-specific rules not read; text says 'your state's law'. Added 2026-11-16 from the §4.4 persona pass (ADV-45). Checker 2026-11-16: block text scoped to collectors ('If a collector asks you to pay'), as the CFPB page is.

new_claims.claim: For the mother's or father's benefit, a child in care who is 16 or older and not disabled is treated as not entitled to child's benefits, so the any-age survivor benefit requires a child under 16 or disabled
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: §402(s)(1) ('For the purposes of subsections (b)(1), (c)(1), (g)(1) ... a child who is entitled to child's insurance benefits ... and who has attained the age of 16 but is not in such month under a disability ... shall be deemed not entitled to such benefits'). Refines CL534. Added 2026-11-16 from the §4.4 persona pass (ADV-46, CFP-46).
